newsitem.title: USA: GM Oklahoma plant gets UAW strike deadline.
newsitem.headline: GM Oklahoma plant gets UAW strike deadline.

text.p: The United Auto Workers, threatening General Motors Corp. with another plant shutdown, Wednesday set a strike deadline at the automaker's key Oklahoma City car assembly plant.
UAW Local 1999 said about 3,600 members would strike the plant at 11:59 p.m. EST on April 4, if union and GM negotiators fail to reach a tentative agreement for a new local labor contract.
The plant is the main production source for two important new GM mid-size cars, the Chevrolet Malibu and the Oldsmobile Cutlass.

A strike at the plant would deprive GM dealers of the cars just as national television advertising campaigns worth tens of millions of dollars are beginning to break. The Malibu and Cutlass, developed under the code-name "P-90" are a cornerstone of GM's efforts to regain market share in the U.S. intermediate car segment, which it once dominated.
Local 1999 said in a statement that eight months of negotiations with GM have failed to resolve a major dispute over the number of workers needed in the plant.

"With the introduction of the P-90, management decided that we needed far less people, therefore the number of workers in the plant has been substantially reduced," the union said in a statement. "The effect is increasing workloads of individual workers resulting in an alarming rate of repetitive trauma injuries."

GM spokesman James Farmer said the union agreed to create certain efficiencies when it made a business case to persuade GM to build the P-90 cars at the plant, and the company wants to ensure those benefits are preserved.
"Some of the things that we agreed upon when they built that business case are now issues in the talks," Farmer said. "Some of it was around manpower."
Farmer said GM was disappointed that the UAW threatened to strike, but he added that the company remains hopeful that the disputes can be resolved without a work stoppage.
"Hopefully, we'll have the cars to sell," he said.

The Oklahoma City plant, which has never had a strike in its 18-year history, recently launched production of the all-new Cutlass and Malibu and is up to about 80 percent of its full production capacity. A second plant, in Wilmington, Del., just began production of Malibus about two weeks ago, but is much further behind on its launch curve.

Meanwhile, GM and the UAW are continuing talks to end a 12-day-old strike at a full-size pickup truck plant in Fort Wayne, Ind. Union officials reported that little progress has been made in those negotiations.
GM has three other North American plants that build its popular full-size C/K pickup trucks.
